name: Regulatory T cell
summary: A CD4 T cell whose job is to keep immune responses in check. Defined by the transcription factor FOXP3, regulatory T cells restrain other T cells, dendritic cells and B-cell responses, which protects the body's own tissues and limits damage after infection. Most are made in the thymus; people with no working FOXP3 gene develop severe autoimmune disease.
functions: Develops mostly in the thymus: CD4 thymocytes whose receptor binds a self-peptide on MHC class II fairly strongly, with IL-2 to support them, switch on FOXP3 instead of dying. Mouse experiments show this needs both medullary epithelial cells and dendritic cells, and that regulatory T cells that have already left later return to the thymus, where they hold back the making of new ones (shown in mice and in human thymus tissue).
Depends on FOXP3 as its master gene: mutations in it cause the fatal autoimmune syndrome IPEX in boys, and the scurfy mouse, with a matching mutation, dies of runaway T-cell activation.

Restrains other cells by contact and competition: CTLA-4 on its surface strips CD80 and CD86 off dendritic cells, so they co-stimulate poorly, and its high CD25 (the IL-2 receptor α chain) soaks up the IL-2 that activated T cells need. The IL-2 competition is shown mainly in mouse and culture experiments.

Restrains by secretion: releases IL-10 and TGF-β, which damp inflammation, especially at the skin, gut and lung surfaces. A third inhibitory cytokine, IL-35, contributes in mice but is much less clear in humans.

Matches its control to the response: regulatory T cells that switch on T-bet restrain Th1 responses, those that use IRF4 restrain Th2 responses, those that use STAT3 restrain Th17 responses, and a subset carrying CXCR5 and BCL6 (follicular regulatory T cells) enters germinal centres to restrain Tfh and B cells. Mostly shown in mice.

Lives in tissues as well as lymphoid organs: regulatory T cells in mouse muscle and fat help repair and metabolism, and almost all the regulatory T cells in healthy human skin have a memory phenotype. Some tissue regulatory T cells respond to antigens made locally.

Debated: how many regulatory T cells come from the thymus and how many are induced from naive CD4 T cells in the body (with TGF-β and IL-2, especially in the gut). Helios and neuropilin-1 were proposed as markers that tell them apart in mice, but Helios also rises when T cells are activated, and neuropilin-1 has been tested mainly in mice.

Debated: how stable the cell is. Some mouse experiments find that cells that lose FOXP3 can become harmful effector T cells; others find the lineage stable and the effect small. The answer matters for using regulatory T cells as therapy.

Debated: how to recognise them in humans. Activated human T cells that are not regulatory also switch on FOXP3 briefly, so FOXP3 alone can mislabel them; combining CD25 high, CD127 low and other markers helps, but the best definition is still argued.
abundance: About 5-10% of CD4 T cells in adult human blood (identified as CD25-high, CD127-low and FOXP3-positive); the share is often higher in tissues such as skin. In mice about 10-15% of CD4 T cells in lymph nodes and spleen are FOXP3-positive, though figures vary with age and strain.
